blocks.text: The narrator does not explain why Mordecai refuses to bow to Haman. Suggestions based on religious law, personal defiance, or the contrast between Mordecai’s Benjaminite ancestry and Haman’s title “Agagite” remain possibilities, not stated reasons. What the chapter does make plain is Haman’s disproportionate response: he turns a conflict with one man into a plan to destroy Mordecai’s entire people, using a lot to select the date and portraying the Jews to the king as a threatening, dispersed people.

The chapter’s threat is directed against Jews as a people, not merely against Mordecai. The sealed order is sent rapidly through the kingdom in the languages of its provinces, making its intended reach unmistakably broad. Later in the book, the first edict is treated as unable to be withdrawn, so the crisis is addressed through a second authorization. This helps explain why the administrative details in verses 12–15 are not incidental: they show how a personal act of wrath becomes an empire-wide danger.

Across Esther, detailed Persian court color appears alongside stylized storytelling, irony, repeated improbabilities, symmetry, and reversals. Different descriptions of the book—such as history, court tale, comedy, or historical novella—highlight real features but do not settle every historical question. Readers also encounter materially different forms of Esther: the Greek versions expand and interpret the story with dreams, prayers, divine naming, and fuller documents.
